topics.kicker: Kingdom of molds, yeasts, mushrooms · Decomposers with no chlorophyll
topics.dates: Classified as its own kingdom in 1969
topics.briefing: Mushrooms, molds, yeasts, and truffles might look like plants, but fungi actually form their own kingdom of life. Lacking chlorophyll, most fungi feed by decomposing dead matter or by forming partnerships with plant roots called mycorrhizae. Unlike a plant’s cellulose walls, a fungal cell wall is built from a tough material called chitin, the same substance found in insect shells.

trap.title: Fungi, or just a plant?
trap.body: Mushrooms and molds look plant-like and do not move, but they are not plants — they cannot make their own food, since they lack chlorophyll entirely. Their cell walls are also built differently: chitin here, versus cellulose in a true plant’s cell wall. A lichen, built from a fungus paired with algae, is a different combined organism, not this kingdom alone.
trap.fix: If clues mention chlorophyll, photosynthesis, or cellulose cell walls, that points to a plant or alga, not this kingdom. If clues mention chitin cell walls, hyphae, mycorrhizae, decomposing dead matter, or no chlorophyll at all, that points here.

topics.kicker: Simple sugar cells break down for energy · The body’s main fuel
topics.briefing: Glucose is a simple sugar that serves as the body’s main source of energy, broken down inside cells during a process called glycolysis. Plants build it directly during photosynthesis, while animals get it by digesting carbohydrates like starch and rely on insulin to usher it from the blood into cells. Too much glucose lingering in the blood, as in diabetes, can damage organs over time.

topics.name: Ribosomes
topics.kicker: Tiny organelles that build proteins · Read mRNA to link amino acids
topics.dates: First identified by George Palade in 1955
topics.briefing: Ribosomes are the cell’s tiny protein factories, each one reading a strand of messenger RNA like an instruction manual and linking amino acids together one by one. Built from two subunits assembled in the nucleolus, they can float freely in the cytoplasm or stud the rough endoplasmic reticulum like tiny rivets. Every living cell, from bacteria to blue whales, is packed with thousands of them, because every cell constantly needs fresh protein.

tossups.p: The sedimentation rates of this structure’s two subunits are measured in Svedberg units, with bacterial versions showing 30S and 50S values that combine into a 70S whole. A bridge called B2a, containing a segment named Helix 69, is a target for aminoglycoside [“uh-MEE-no-GLY-co-side”] antibiotics within this structure.
tossups.r: Elongation factors such as EF-Tu escort transfer RNA molecules into the A site, the entry point among this structure’s A, P, and E sites. For 10 points, name these organelles, assembled in the nucleolus, that read messenger RNA to build chains of amino acids.

tossups.p: A technique that “freezes” these structures in place with the drug cycloheximide [“sy-kloh-HEX-ih-mide”] is called profiling, letting scientists see exactly which messenger RNA sequences are being read at a given moment. This structure’s core job, linking amino acids with a peptide bond, is carried out by an RNA-based enzyme called peptidyl transferase.
tossups.r: Chloramphenicol and tetracycline block this structure’s function in bacteria while largely sparing human cells. For 10 points, name these tiny structures where proteins are assembled.

tossups.p: Signal recognition particles guide this structure toward a channel called the Sec61 translocon [“trans-LOH-con”] whenever a growing protein carries a signal sequence. This structure cycles between a free, unbound state and one docked at that channel.
tossups.r: This structure’s job halts when a release factor recognizes one of three stop sequences nicknamed amber, ochre, and opal. For 10 points, name these organelles that build proteins by reading messenger RNA three letters at a time.

tossups.p: This structure’s own folded strand of RNA is often cited as key evidence for the “RNA World” hypothesis about life’s earliest chemistry. A condensation reaction inside this structure joins a free amine group on one amino acid to a carboxyl group on the next, releasing water as it forms each new bond in a growing chain.
tossups.r: Tetracycline binds to this structure and blocks protein-making in bacteria. For 10 points, name this organelle, built partly from RNA, where amino acids are strung together.

topics.kicker: Rigid layer outside plant, fungal, and bacterial cells · Gives them shape
topics.dates: Robert Hooke glimpsed these in cork cells in 1665
topics.briefing: A cell wall is a tough, rigid layer wrapped around the outside of plant, fungal, and bacterial cells, giving them a fixed shape and keeping them from bursting as they soak up water. Plant walls are built from cellulose, fungal ones from chitin, and bacterial ones from peptidoglycan, three completely different materials doing the same sturdy job. Animal cells never grow one, a big reason your skin cells are so much squishier than a leaf.

tossups.p: Lysozyme, an enzyme found in tears and egg white, defends against bacteria by hydrolyzing the bond between two alternating sugar units, N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine, that link into long chains within this structure. tossups.r: DD-transpeptidases cross-link sugar strands within this layer, a process penicillin blocks. For 10 points, name this rigid structure that surrounds a bacterial cell’s plasma membrane.

tossups.p: Suberin-rich bands called Casparian strips form part of this structure in plant roots, blocking water from slipping between neighboring cells. A pectin-rich middle lamella glues together adjacent plant cells’ versions of this structure from the outside.
tossups.r: Channels called plasmodesmata [“plaz-moh-DEZ-muh-tuh”] tunnel through this layer, letting the cytoplasm of neighboring plant cells stay connected. For 10 points, name this rigid structure that surrounds a plant cell’s membrane, made of cellulose.

tossups.p: During plant cell division, a structure called the phragmoplast grows outward from leftover spindle fibers and lays down a disc called the cell plate, which matures into this structure. This layer lets a plant cell survive soaking up extra water by physically resisting turgor pressure instead of bursting.
tossups.r: Collenchyma and sclerenchyma plant tissues are defined partly by how thick and stiff this structure is. For 10 points, name this rigid layer that keeps plant cells from swelling and popping, built from cellulose.

tossups.p: The polysaccharide xylan is woven into this structure, making it harder for enzymes to break down, and a pectin-rich middle lamella forms its outermost layer in plants. Gram staining measures how much peptidoglycan this structure contains in bacteria, sorting them into Gram-positive and Gram-negative groups.
tossups.r: This layer is built from cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi, and peptidoglycan in bacteria. For 10 points, name this rigid structure that is completely absent in animal cells.

tossups.p: An outer S-layer made of protein can sit directly atop this structure in some bacteria and archaea. Lignin, the tough compound that stiffens wood, builds up heavily in a secondary, thickened version of this structure in woody plant tissue.
tossups.r: Plasmodesmata tunnel through this layer to connect the cytoplasm of neighboring plant cells. For 10 points, name this structure, found outside the cell membrane of plants, fungi, and bacteria, but never animals.

tossups.p: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin and cephalosporins fight bacterial infections by blocking enzymes that cross-link this structure, causing it to fail and the cell to burst. Echinocandin antifungal drugs instead target the fungal version of this layer the same way.
tossups.r: Crystal violet dye either stays trapped in this layer or rinses away during Gram staining, the classic test for classifying bacteria. For 10 points, name this rigid structure built partly from peptidoglycan in bacteria.

tossups.p: Among bacteria, mycoplasma are unusual for lacking this structure entirely, leaving them without its usual protection. In some other bacteria, a waxy coating of mycolic acid is layered onto this structure, helping them resist staining and some antibiotics.
tossups.r: This structure’s thickness, measured by how well it holds onto crystal violet dye, determines whether a bacterium is classified as Gram-positive or Gram-negative. For 10 points, name this rigid barrier that surrounds a bacterial cell’s plasma membrane.

tossups.p: Collenchyma, sclerenchyma, and parenchyma, three types of plant tissue, are partly told apart by how thick and rigid this structure is in each one. Lignin builds up heavily in a secondary, extra-sturdy version of this layer in woody plant tissue.
tossups.r: This structure resists turgor pressure, the outward push of water inside the cell, keeping a plant cell from bursting instead of just swelling. For 10 points, name this rigid structure made of cellulose in plants.

tossups.p: A pectin-rich layer called the middle lamella glues together neighboring plant cells’ versions of this structure from the outside. Channels called plasmodesmata tunnel straight through this layer, letting the cytoplasm of adjacent plant cells stay connected.
tossups.r: This structure is made of chitin in fungi and peptidoglycan in bacteria, but cellulose in plants. For 10 points, name this rigid layer that is completely missing from animal cells.

tossups.p: This structure resists the outward push of water inside the cell, called turgor pressure, letting a plant cell stay firm instead of bursting when it soaks up extra water. Found in bacteria, fungi, and plants, this layer is one of the clearest differences between a plant cell and an animal cell under a microscope.
tossups.r: Plants build this structure from cellulose, fungi from chitin, and bacteria from peptidoglycan. For 10 points, name this rigid layer that is completely absent from animal cells.

tossups.p: Bactoprenol ferries peptidoglycan building blocks across a bacterium’s inner membrane so they can be added onto this growing structure. DD-transpeptidase enzymes then stitch those new strands into the existing structure, cross-linking them together.
tossups.r: Beta-lactam antibiotics like penicillin work by jamming that cross-linking step in this layer. For 10 points, name this structure, found outside a bacterial cell’s plasma membrane.

tossups.p: Alternating sugar units called NAM and NAG link together into long chains called peptidoglycan that make up this structure in bacteria. Gram-positive bacteria pack far more peptidoglycan into this layer than Gram-negative bacteria do.
tossups.r: Lysozyme, an enzyme found in tears and egg whites, defends against infection by breaking down this structure. For 10 points, name this rigid barrier surrounding a bacterial cell’s plasma membrane.

tossups.p: This structure is missing from mycoplasma bacteria and from every animal cell, but present in plants, fungi, and most other bacteria. It gives a cell a fixed shape and keeps it from swelling up and bursting when water rushes in.
tossups.r: Plant versions of this layer are built from cellulose, fungal versions from chitin, and bacterial versions from peptidoglycan. For 10 points, name this rigid structure that surrounds a cell’s membrane.

trap.title: Cell wall, or cell membrane?
trap.body: This is one of the most common middle-school mix-ups in cell biology: every cell has a cell membrane, but plant, fungal, and bacterial cells also have this extra, rigid outer layer. Several real tossups for this structure explicitly warn “do not accept or prompt on cell membrane,” since describing one while asking for the other is a classic trap.

If the clues mention rigidity, a specific building material (cellulose, chitin, or peptidoglycan), Gram staining, or something surrounding the cell membrane itself, that is this structure.

topics.name: Evolution
topics.kicker: Change in species over generations · Driven mainly by natural selection
topics.dates: On the Origin of Species published 1859
topics.briefing: Evolution is the gradual change in a population’s inherited traits across many generations, the process that explains why Earth’s millions of living things are all related yet so different. Charles Darwin proposed that it happens mainly through natural selection, in which organisms with helpful traits survive and reproduce more often, slowly reshaping a population over time. Darwin built his case partly on finch beaks he studied on the Galápagos Islands.

tossups.p: According to the Hardy-Weinberg principle, a population would stop undergoing this process entirely if five conditions were all met at once, including random mating, an infinite population size, and no migration between groups. Violating even one of those conditions is enough to drive this process forward.
tossups.r: Charles Lyell’s _Principles of Geology_ convinced Charles Darwin that Earth was old enough for this gradual process to reshape life. For 10 points, name this process by which species change across many generations.

tossups.p: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck wrongly proposed that this process was driven mainly by the “use” or “disuse” of an organism’s organs during its own lifetime. Reading Charles Lyell’s _Principles of Geology_ convinced one later scientist that Earth was old enough for this gradual process to reshape life over millions of years.
tossups.r: Studying finch beaks on the Galápagos Islands helped Charles Darwin work out how this process happens. For 10 points, name this process that changes a species’ inherited traits over many generations.

tossups.p: Richard Dawkins promoted a gene-centered view of this process and coined the term “meme” to describe a cultural, idea-based form of it. This process drives the “convergent” development of similar traits in unrelated species, such as the wings of birds and bats.
tossups.r: Darwin proposed that this process happens mainly through natural selection. For 10 points, name this gradual process by which species change over generations.

tossups.p: Naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace independently worked out a theory of this process while studying wildlife in the Malay Archipelago, arriving at conclusions strikingly close to another scientist’s unpublished ideas. The two men’s papers on this process were presented jointly in 1858, pushing the more famous scientist to finally publish his own book the next year.
tossups.r: That scientist, Charles Darwin, collected finches on the Galápagos Islands whose varied beaks became famous evidence for this process. For 10 points, name this process described in Darwin’s _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: Philosopher Herbert Spencer coined the phrase “survival of the fittest” to describe this process, a phrase Charles Darwin later adopted himself. This process can speed up dramatically in a lab or hospital setting, as when bacteria rapidly gain resistance to antibiotics over just a few generations.
tossups.r: Darwin proposed that this gradual process happens mainly through natural selection acting on random variation. For 10 points, name this process by which species change across generations.

tossups.p: In the mid-1900s, the “modern synthesis” combined Darwin’s original ideas about this process with Gregor Mendel’s laws of inheritance, finally explaining exactly how new traits get passed on. This process requires heritable variation within a population for natural selection to act upon at all.
tossups.r: Mutations, genetic drift, gene flow, and natural selection are the four main mechanisms that drive this process. For 10 points, name this process by which populations of organisms change over successive generations.

tossups.p: A famous case study of peppered moths in industrial England showed this process in action within just a few human generations, as soot-darkened trees favored darker-colored moths over lighter ones. This same process can be observed happening quickly whenever a population faces a sudden new source of pressure on its survival.
tossups.r: Charles Darwin proposed that this process happens mainly through natural selection. For 10 points, name this process that changes a population’s inherited traits over time.

tossups.p: Bacteria exposed to antibiotics can undergo a fast, observable version of this process within a human lifetime, as drug-resistant strains survive and multiply while others die off. Breeders steer this process on purpose by choosing which plants or animals get to reproduce, a practice called artificial selection.
tossups.r: Charles Darwin proposed natural selection as the main driver of this gradual process. For 10 points, name this process that reshapes a species’ inherited traits across generations.

tossups.p: Unrelated species independently developing strikingly similar traits, like dolphins and sharks both growing streamlined fins, is called the “convergent” form of this process. A “divergent” version of this process instead produces increasingly different traits among related populations, such as Darwin’s famous finches.
tossups.r: Charles Lyell’s ideas about Earth’s great age helped convince Darwin that this slow process had enough time to work. For 10 points, name this process that changes species over long stretches of time.

tossups.p: Because every living thing ultimately shares common ancestors, scientists draw branching diagrams called phylogenetic trees to map out the history of this process. Shared features across very different living things, from the genetic code to basic cell structures, are often cited as strong evidence that this process has occurred.
tossups.r: Charles Darwin described this process as “descent with modification” in his most famous book. For 10 points, name this process that explains how today’s millions of species are all related.

tossups.p: Layers of fossils showing gradual change in similar body shapes over millions of years make up the fossil record, often cited as strong evidence for this process. Comparing similar bone structures across very different animals, like a bat’s wing and a human arm, is called comparative anatomy, another classic line of evidence for this process.
tossups.r: Charles Darwin spent years gathering evidence for this process before finally publishing his ideas. For 10 points, name this process that gradually changes species across generations.

tossups.p: A young naturalist aboard the survey ship HMS _Beagle_ spent years collecting specimens across South America and the Pacific, building the evidence base for a famous theory about this process. Differences among finch beaks on the Galápagos Islands later became one of this scientist’s most famous pieces of evidence.
tossups.r: That naturalist, Charles Darwin, proposed that this process happens mainly through natural selection. For 10 points, name this process, the subject of Darwin’s 1859 book _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: Charles Darwin originally called this process “descent with modification” in the book that introduced his theory to the world. Alfred Russel Wallace independently reached similar conclusions about this process, and the two scientists’ papers were first presented together in 1858.
tossups.r: This process is driven mainly by natural selection, in which organisms with helpful traits survive and reproduce more often. For 10 points, name this process, described in Darwin’s _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: Four main mechanisms drive this process: natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow between populations, and new mutations arising in DNA. The Hardy-Weinberg principle describes the unusual, idealized conditions under which none of these mechanisms would act and a population would stop undergoing this process altogether.
tossups.r: Charles Darwin proposed that this process happens mainly through natural selection, acting on random variation across generations. For 10 points, name this process by which species change over time.

tossups.p: This process explains why every living thing on Earth, from bacteria to blue whales, is related yet so different from one another. It happens when a population’s inherited traits gradually change across many generations, often because individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more successfully.
tossups.r: Charles Darwin described this process in his 1859 book _On the Origin of Species_, proposing natural selection as its main driver. For 10 points, name this gradual process by which species change over time.

topics.name: Lungs
topics.kicker: Paired breathing organs · Where oxygen enters the blood
topics.dates: About 12–20 breaths a minute at rest
topics.briefing: Every breath pulls air down the trachea, through branching bronchi, and into roughly 300 million tiny sacs called alveoli, where oxygen slips into the blood and carbon dioxide slips out. A soapy coating called surfactant keeps those sacs from collapsing between breaths, while a tough covering called the pleura cuts down friction as the lungs expand and contract. Diseases like asthma and emphysema make the job harder by narrowing airways or destroying those delicate sacs.

tossups.p: In amphibians, these organs are filled through buccal pumping rather than rib movements. A “book” version of these organs in arachnids uses hemolymph-filled plates instead of branching airways. In humans, the left and right sides add up to five lobes total, all wrapped in a protective pleural membrane.
tossups.r: Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the heart to capillaries surrounding tiny sacs at the end of each bronchiole. For 10 points, name these paired organs that trade oxygen for carbon dioxide with the blood.

tossups.p: Emphysema and COPD primarily damage these organs by destroying or narrowing their tiny air sacs and airways. A coating called pulmonary surfactant, made by type II cells, keeps those sacs from collapsing by lowering surface tension.
tossups.r: An inhaled medicine called albuterol can relax the airway spasms of asthma, another disease of these organs. For 10 points, name the organs where alveoli let oxygen enter the blood during breathing.

tossups.p: During an asthma attack, the bronchi inside these organs tighten in spasms that an albuterol inhaler can relax. Deoxygenated blood reaches these organs through the pulmonary artery, the only artery in the body that doesn’t carry oxygen-rich blood.
tossups.r: A tough covering called the pleural membrane wraps each of these organs and reduces friction as they expand. For 10 points, name these organs that fill with air through the trachea and bronchi.

tossups.p: Capillaries here hold much of the body’s angiotensin-converting enzyme, which turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II. Type II cells in these organs secrete surfactant, rich in a phospholipid called DPPC, to cut the surface tension of tiny air sacs.
tossups.r: These paired organs are measured with a device called a spirometer. For 10 points, name these organs that branch from the trachea into bronchi and finally into alveoli.

tossups.p: A shunt called the foramen of Panizza lets blood bypass these organs entirely in crocodiles. Premature infants who cannot yet make enough surfactant in these organs can develop a dangerous condition called hyaline membrane disease.
tossups.r: Each half of this pair is wrapped in its own pleural sac. For 10 points, name these organs where tiny sacs called alveoli handle gas exchange.

tossups.p: A calcified scar in these organs, paired with a swollen lymph node, together form what’s called a Ghon [“GOHN”] complex, a sign of past tuberculosis. Capillaries in these organs also carry much of the enzyme that converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a hormone that raises blood pressure.
tossups.r: A spirometer can measure how much air these organs can hold and move. For 10 points, name these two organs, each wrapped in a pleural membrane.

tossups.p: A spirometer measures the vital capacity and tidal volume of these organs. Two separate pleural sacs surround the left and right halves of this pair, letting them expand somewhat independently of each other.
tossups.r: These organs sit just above the diaphragm, the muscle that drives most of the work of breathing. For 10 points, name these organs that fill with air at the trachea and branch down to the alveoli.

tossups.p: As a person ages, the residual volume of these organs rises while their vital capacity falls. A protective coating keeps the tiny sacs inside these organs from collapsing as they shrink back down after each breath.
tossups.r: These organs are surrounded by a pleural membrane whose negative pressure keeps them inflated between breaths. For 10 points, name these paired organs that take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

tossups.p: The pleural membrane around these organs relies on negative pressure, rather than muscle alone, to keep them inflated between breaths. These organs also sit directly above the diaphragm, whose contractions help pull air into their branching airways.
tossups.r: A device called a spirometer measures how much air moves through these organs with each breath. For 10 points, name these organs connected to the outside world through the trachea.

tossups.p: A fast-growing cancer called small-cell carcinoma usually begins in these organs. On the oxygen-hemoglobin saturation curve, blood leaving these organs sits on the high-oxygen side of the graph, since gas exchange there loads hemoglobin up with oxygen.
tossups.r: Capillaries surrounding the alveoli inside these organs pick up oxygen and drop off carbon dioxide. For 10 points, name these paired organs targeted by diseases like emphysema and small-cell carcinoma.

tossups.p: Frogs inflate these organs using positive pressure, pushing air in, while humans use negative pressure to pull air in. Intercostal muscles between the ribs work together with the diaphragm to change the volume of these organs during breathing.
tossups.r: Air entering these organs travels through the trachea, then the bronchi, before reaching tiny sacs called alveoli. For 10 points, name these organs, the site of gas exchange with the blood.

tossups.p: The surfactant DPPC is released by septal cells inside these organs specifically to reduce the surface tension of their alveoli. Air reaches those alveoli only after passing through the trachea and then branching through the bronchi.
tossups.r: Deoxygenated blood travels from the heart to these organs by way of the pulmonary artery. For 10 points, name these spongy organs that handle breathing.

tossups.p: A “book” version of these organs, built from flat, hemolymph-filled plates, lets spiders and other arachnids breathe without ribs at all. Amphibians instead fill true versions of these organs using throat movements called buccal pumping.
tossups.r: In humans, this pair totals five lobes and sits above the diaphragm. For 10 points, name these paired organs wrapped in a pleural membrane.

tossups.p: Hyaline membrane disease can strike these organs in premature babies who haven’t yet made enough surfactant. A Ghon complex, combining a calcified scar in these organs with a nearby swollen lymph node, can mark an old, healed case of tuberculosis.
tossups.r: These organs are each wrapped in a protective pleural sac. For 10 points, name these organs that branch into bronchi and alveoli.

tossups.p: Conditions such as emphysema, COPD, and asthma all make it harder for these organs to move air in and out. A soapy coating called surfactant, produced inside these organs, keeps their smallest air sacs from sticking shut.
tossups.r: These organs trade carbon dioxide for oxygen with blood arriving through the pulmonary artery. For 10 points, name these two organs that fill the chest on either side of the heart.

clues.t: Paired organs that trade oxygen for carbon dioxide with the blood during breathing
Air branches from the trachea through bronchi down to tiny sacs called alveoli
Wrapped in a protective double layer called the pleural membrane, or pleura
Conditions like asthma, emphysema, and COPD make it harder for these organs to work
A soapy coating called surfactant, made by type II cells, keeps tiny air sacs from collapsing
Sit just above the diaphragm, the muscle that drives most of the work of breathing
A device called a spirometer measures how much air these organs can hold and move
The pulmonary artery is the only artery in the body that carries oxygen-poor blood
Premature babies who can’t make enough surfactant can develop hyaline membrane disease
A hemolymph-filled “book” version of these organs lets spiders and other arachnids breathe
Amphibians fill theirs using throat movements called buccal pumping instead of chest muscles
A fast-growing cancer called small-cell carcinoma usually starts in these organs
In humans, the right and left sides together add up to five lobes
Capillaries here hold much of the body’s angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
That enzyme converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II, which raises blood pressure
In crocodiles, a shunt called the foramen of Panizza lets blood bypass these organs
A calcified tuberculosis scar here, plus a swollen lymph node, form a Ghon complex
The pleural membrane creates negative pressure that keeps these organs inflated between breaths
With age, residual volume rises while vital capacity falls
On the oxygen-hemoglobin saturation curve, blood leaving these organs sits on the high-oxygen side
Frogs inflate theirs using positive pressure to push air in, unlike humans, who pull air in with negative pressure
Intercostal muscles between the ribs work with the diaphragm to change their volume

trap.title: Heart, or lungs?
trap.body: Many tossups describe blood flowing from the heart through the pulmonary artery, which can tempt a player to buzz “heart” as soon as that word appears. But the pulmonary artery is only the delivery route — the organ actually being described, where that blood meets air and trades carbon dioxide for oxygen, is these paired organs. A second trap: the “book lungs” of spiders and scorpions are a real but very different structure built from flat, hemolymph-filled plates instead of branching airways.
trap.fix: If the clues mention the heart only as the source of blood arriving by the pulmonary artery, keep listening — the real answer is whatever organ actually receives and uses that blood. Only answer “book lungs” if the question is specifically about arachnids.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lungs (accept book lungs; prompt on respiratory system; do not accept heart)

topics.name: Neurons
topics.kicker: Signal-carrying nerve cells · The nervous system’s basic units
topics.dates: An estimated 86 billion in the human brain
topics.briefing: Neurons are the body’s messengers, firing tiny electrical pulses called action potentials down a long fiber called the axon and passing the signal to the next cell across a gap called a synapse. A fatty coating called myelin, built by helper cells, wraps many axons like the insulation on a wire, speeding those signals along. Scientist Santiago Ramón y Cajal helped prove that neurons are separate, individual cells rather than one continuous web.
topics.answerHtml: Neurons (accept nerve cells; prompt on nerves; do not accept “axons” or “brain”)

sample.note: 9 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (1 Middle School/Easy High School + 8 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: A kind of these cells with just two branches leaving its cell body is called “bipolar.” Supporting cells, including oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, surround and protect these cells. Their myelin coating, which has gaps called Nodes of Ranvier, is damaged in the disease multiple sclerosis.
tossups.r: These cells release chemical messengers like acetylcholine or serotonin into gaps called synapses. For 10 points, name these functional cells of the nervous system, which send signals along a long fiber toward other cells’ dendrites.

tossups.p: These cells’ development is guided by a structure called a growth cone, built from actin fibers. A once-popular but incorrect “reticular” theory claiming these cells form one continuous web was disproved by Santiago Ramón y Cajal [“rah-MOHN ee kah-HAL”], who studied them using a silver-staining method invented by Camillo Golgi.
tossups.r: The Hodgkin-Huxley model, based on a squid’s giant axon, explains how ion channels create an electrical signal. For 10 points, name these signal-carrying cells of the nervous system.

tossups.p: Granular structures called Nissl bodies, made of rough endoplasmic reticulum, appear inside these cells under a microscope. These cells can be sorted into afferent, efferent, and “inter-” types based on which direction they carry signals.
tossups.r: A fatty sheath made of myelin, built by oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells, speeds up the signals these cells send. For 10 points, name these cells that use a long axon and branching dendrites to communicate.

tossups.p: Camillo Golgi separated a many-branched, multipolar type of these cells into two groups and also stained the “Purkinje” variety, found in dense numbers in the cerebellum. A doctrine named for these cells established that they are separate, individual units rather than one continuous chain.
tossups.r: A sodium-potassium pump helps restore these cells’ resting electrical charge after each signal fires. For 10 points, name these cells that send and receive signals at junctions called synapses.

tossups.p: Vesicle fusion inside these cells depends on SNARE proteins called VAMP1 and VAMP2. The skin of naked mole rats was found to lack a pain-signaling peptide, Substance P, that these cells normally secrete. A “black reaction” stain for these cells, using silver nitrate, is named for Camillo Golgi.
tossups.r: A fatty substance called myelin speeds up the electrical signals that travel along these cells. For 10 points, name these basic signaling units of the nervous system.

tossups.p: New copies of these cells are still produced in adulthood within brain regions called the dentate gyrus and the subventricular zone. In the disease Guillain-Barré [“ghee-YAN bah-RAY”] syndrome, the immune system attacks the protective coating of these cells outside the brain and spinal cord.
tossups.r: These cells release neurotransmitters such as glutamate and GABA at synapses. For 10 points, name these cells, built from a cell body, dendrites, and an axon, that make up the nervous system.

tossups.p: A disordered protein called alpha-synuclein can build up inside these cells in Parkinson’s disease. These cells are coated by a fatty substance produced by oligodendrocytes, and supporting cells called glia help keep them healthy throughout the body.
tossups.r: These cells release glutamate, GABA, and other chemical messengers at synapses. For 10 points, name these cells that transmit signals throughout the nervous system.

tossups.p: The material covering part of these cells is rich in a lipid called galactocerebroside, and new ones can form in the subventricular and subgranular zones even in adults. In simple animals called cnidarians, these cells form a loose web called a nerve net instead of a brain.
tossups.r: Sodium-potassium pumps in these cells’ membranes help generate traveling electrical signals called action potentials. For 10 points, name these cells made of a soma, dendrites, and an axon.

tossups.p: The rough endoplasmic reticulum inside these cells shows up under a blue dye called the Nissl stain. Along their myelin-wrapped fibers, extracellular fluid touches these cells only at gaps called Nodes of Ranvier, allowing a faster, hopping style of signal transmission called saltatory conduction.
tossups.r: Supporting cells such as oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells coat these cells in a fatty myelin sheath. For 10 points, name these cells, separated from each other by synapses, that feature dendrites and an axon.

tossups.p: A special case of the telegrapher’s equation, using the square of a “length constant,” can model the electrical behavior of these cells. Star-shaped supporting cells called astrocytes help blood vessels near these cells form a protective barrier, and a stain developed by Golgi using potassium dichromate can reveal an “inter-” variety of these cells.
tossups.r: An action potential travels down a long fiber of these cells, itself wrapped in a myelin sheath. For 10 points, name these cells of the nervous system that transport electrical impulses.

tossups.p: Hodgkin and Huxley studied a squid’s giant axon to work out how ion channels produce an electrical signal in these cells. The migration of these cells during development happens along supporting structures called radial glia.
tossups.r: Depending on where they sit in the body, these cells can be insulated by either Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes. For 10 points, name these cells that contain a soma, dendrites, and an axon.

tossups.p: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system damages the fatty coating that normally speeds up the signals sent by these cells. A sodium-potassium pump helps restore these cells’ resting voltage after each signal, called an action potential, fires along their length.
tossups.r: These cells pass signals to the next cell across a tiny gap called a synapse. For 10 points, name these cells, which include “inter-,” afferent, and efferent types, that make up the nervous system.

tossups.p: Golgi’s silver-staining method, later improved by Santiago Ramón y Cajal, first let scientists see the true branching shape of these cells clearly enough to disprove the old “reticular” theory. These cells rely on a sodium-potassium pump to reset their electrical charge between signals.
tossups.r: A fatty myelin sheath, built by Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes, insulates the long signaling fiber of these cells. For 10 points, name these electrically active cells of the nervous system.

tossups.p: In the ocean-dwelling cnidarians, these cells form a loose, brainless “nerve net” rather than a centralized organ. A growth cone made of actin fibers guides these cells as they develop and make new connections.
tossups.r: These cells communicate using chemical messengers such as acetylcholine, glutamate, and GABA. For 10 points, name these cells, which include bipolar, multipolar, and “inter-” varieties, that carry signals through the body.

tossups.p: Nissl bodies, Golgi’s silver stain, and a myelin coating supplied by Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes are all features used to study and identify these cells under a microscope. These cells’ resting electrical charge is restored after each signal by a sodium-potassium pump.
tossups.r: These cells send action potentials down a long fiber and receive them through branching dendrites. For 10 points, name these electrically and chemically active cells that make up the body’s nervous system.

clues.t: The nervous system’s basic signaling cells, built from a cell body, dendrites, and an axon
Fire tiny electrical signals called action potentials to communicate with other cells
Pass their signal to the next cell across a tiny gap called a synapse
Together make up the brain, spinal cord, and nerves of the nervous system
A fatty coating called myelin, made by helper cells, speeds up their signals
Schwann cells build that coating in the body; oligodendrocytes build it in the brain and spinal cord
Gaps in that coating, called Nodes of Ranvier, let “saltatory conduction” speed signals along in jumps
A sodium-potassium pump helps reset the cell’s electrical charge after each signal fires
Camillo Golgi developed a silver-staining method that first let scientists see these cells clearly
Santiago Ramón y Cajal used that stain to disprove the idea that these cells form one continuous web
Afferent types carry signals toward the brain and spinal cord; efferent types carry them away; “inter-” types connect the two
Supporting cells called glia, or glial cells, nourish and protect these cells but don’t fire signals themselves
Hodgkin and Huxley studied a squid’s giant axon to explain how ion channels create these cells’ electrical signals
In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks and damages the fatty coating around these cells
In Guillain-Barré syndrome, the immune system instead attacks these cells’ coating outside the brain and spinal cord
New ones are still produced in adulthood in brain regions called the dentate gyrus and subventricular zone
Release chemical messengers such as glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, or serotonin into synapses
Granular structures called Nissl bodies, made of rough endoplasmic reticulum, show up when these cells are stained
A structure called a growth cone, built from actin fibers, guides these cells as they grow and connect
In simple animals called cnidarians, these cells form a loose web called a nerve net instead of a brain
Their electrical behavior along a fiber can be modeled with a version of the telegrapher’s equation
Camillo Golgi’s stain revealed the many-branched “Purkinje” variety of these cells found in the cerebellum

trap.title: Whole cell, axon, or brain?
trap.body: Some real tossups are actually about the axon, the long fiber that carries signals away from one of these cells — those tossups only prompt if a player says the broader cell type. Going the other direction, many of these cells bundled together build the brain and spinal cord, but the brain is a whole organ made of billions of them, not a single one.
trap.fix: If every clue describes one long fiber insulated in myelin and firing a single traveling signal, especially one mentioning a giant squid experiment, the safer answer may be “axon,” a part of one of these cells. If the clues describe thinking, memory, or an organ with lobes, the answer is the brain, not these individual cells.
trap.line: Real answer line: Neurons (accept nerve cells; prompt on nerves; do not accept axons or brain)

topics.name: Nucleus
topics.kicker: Cell’s membrane-bound control center · Houses its genetic material
topics.dates: Named by botanist Robert Brown in 1831
topics.briefing: The nucleus acts like a cell’s command center, holding almost all of its DNA safely inside a double-layered envelope dotted with thousands of pores that let RNA and proteins pass in and out. Inside sits a smaller, darker region called the nucleolus, which builds the ribosomes a cell needs to make proteins. Nearly every eukaryotic cell has a nucleus, while bacteria and other prokaryotes get by without one at all.

sample.note: 5 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked, after excluding 3 off-topic atomic/comet-nucleus hits from the same search)

tossups.p: Speckles, paraspeckles, and Cajal [“kah-HAL”] bodies float inside this organelle’s envelope. A substructure inside it completely dissolves during prophase, then reassembles once mitosis ends, after spending the rest of the cell cycle churning out ribosomes.
tossups.r: Eukaryotic cells are defined by having one of these, while bacteria and other prokaryotes get by without one. For 10 points, name this organelle that houses a cell’s DNA.

tossups.p: A system of pores built into this organelle’s envelope lets ribosomes exit after being assembled in a smaller region inside it. Protein-and-RNA-filled Cajal bodies also float within this structure.
tossups.r: Its outer membrane connects directly to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. For 10 points, name this organelle that acts as a eukaryotic cell’s control center.

tossups.p: Several of these organelles can occupy a single long, connected fungal cell called a hypha [“HIGH-fuh”]. Cajal bodies are found within it, and its envelope stays continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
tossups.r: A subsection of it assembles ribosomes before they’re exported through its pores. For 10 points, name this structure that holds a eukaryotic cell’s genetic material.

tossups.p: This organelle’s envelope is broken down during the prophase stage of mitosis and rebuilt afterward. A subsection of it produces ribosomes, which exit through pores in its membrane.
tossups.r: Prokaryotic cells entirely lack this organelle. For 10 points, name this structure found in eukaryotic cells that stores chromosomes.

tossups.p: snRNPs [“snurps”] inside this organelle splice together pre-messenger RNA, and its namesake pores interact with transport helpers called importin and RanGTP.
tossups.r: Its membrane connects directly to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. For 10 points, name this organelle whose smaller internal region, the nucleolus, assembles ribosomes.

tossups.p: Scottish botanist Robert Brown named and described this structure in 1831, decades before its role in heredity was understood. A mesh of proteins called the lamina lines its inner membrane and helps give it shape.
tossups.r: It is usually the largest organelle inside a eukaryotic cell. For 10 points, name this structure that houses a cell’s DNA.

tossups.p: Dark-staining, tightly packed DNA called heterochromatin tends to cluster along the inside of this organelle’s envelope. Each pore in that envelope is actually a large assembly built from dozens of proteins, called a pore complex.
tossups.r: This organelle’s envelope is really two membranes with a narrow fluid-filled gap between them. For 10 points, name this structure, often called the “control center” of a eukaryotic cell.

tossups.p: In an animal cell, this organelle usually sits near the center, but in a plant cell it can be pushed off to one side by a large central vacuole. A protein called RanGTP helps control which molecules pass through its pores.
tossups.r: Eukaryotic cells are defined by having this organelle, which prokaryotic cells lack. For 10 points, name this structure that contains a cell’s chromosomes.

tossups.p: A smaller, darker region inside this organelle dissolves completely during prophase and reforms once cell division ends. Before it dissolves, that region spends most of the cell cycle assembling ribosomes.
tossups.r: Its envelope connects directly to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. For 10 points, name this organelle, the largest structure inside most eukaryotic cells.

tossups.p: Transport proteins called importins help molecules cross the pores of this organelle’s double membrane. Speckles and paraspeckles, storage spots for RNA-splicing proteins, float inside it alongside Cajal bodies.
tossups.r: This organelle’s envelope breaks down at the start of mitosis. For 10 points, name this structure that keeps a eukaryotic cell’s genetic material separated from the rest of the cell.

tossups.p: This organelle’s outer membrane is studded with ribosomes and connects directly to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, while its inner membrane is lined by a protein mesh called the lamina. Several of these organelles can share one giant fungal cell called a hypha.
tossups.r: A smaller region within it, the nucleolus, builds ribosomal subunits. For 10 points, name this organelle that stores a cell’s DNA inside a protective envelope.

tossups.p: Thousands of pore complexes dot the double membrane of this organelle, regulating traffic in and out. It was described and named by the botanist Robert Brown in 1831.
tossups.r: Eukaryotic cells typically contain one of these; prokaryotic cells like bacteria do not. For 10 points, name this organelle often called the “control center” of the cell.

tossups.p: snRNPs inside this organelle handle the splicing of pre-mRNA before it leaves for the rest of the cell. A thin, fluid-filled space separates the two membranes that make up its envelope.
tossups.r: This organelle breaks down and then rebuilds its envelope once each time a cell divides by mitosis. For 10 points, name this structure that houses chromosomes made of DNA and protein.

tossups.p: Cajal bodies and paraspeckles both occur inside this organelle, whose pores interact with the transport proteins importin and RanGTP. In certain fungi, many of these organelles can share a single long hyphal cell.
tossups.r: A smaller region inside it, called the nucleolus, builds a cell’s ribosomes. For 10 points, name this structure, the largest organelle in most eukaryotic cells.

tossups.p: This organelle’s envelope disappears for part of the cell cycle’s division stage, called mitosis, before reassembling around each new set of chromosomes. Heterochromatin tends to cluster near the inner face of its double membrane.
tossups.r: Bacteria and other prokaryotes lack this membrane-bound organelle entirely. For 10 points, name this structure that acts as a eukaryotic cell’s control center and stores its DNA.

clues.t: A double-layered envelope holds almost all of a eukaryotic cell’s DNA inside this organelle
Present in nearly every eukaryotic cell but missing from simpler prokaryotic cells like bacteria
Thousands of pores in its envelope let RNA and proteins pass in and out
Contains a smaller region, the nucleolus, which builds a cell’s ribosomes
Its envelope breaks down during prophase, the first stage of the cell division called mitosis
Small round structures called Cajal bodies float inside it, alongside paraspeckles
Its outer membrane connects directly to the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Tiny particles called snRNPs inside it splice newly made messenger RNA
Its pores interact with transport helpers called importin and RanGTP
In some fungi, several of these organelles share one long, connected cell called a hypha
Scottish botanist Robert Brown named and described this structure in 1831
Often nicknamed the cell’s “control center” since it directs which proteins get made
Its envelope is actually two membranes with a narrow fluid-filled space between them
Also contains structures called speckles and paraspeckles, storage spots for splicing proteins
A protein called RanGTP helps control which molecules its pores let through
Unlike the rest of it, the nucleolus completely dissolves during prophase before re-forming later
Usually sits near the center of an animal cell but can be pushed to one side in a plant cell
Typically the largest organelle in a eukaryotic cell, often taking up around a tenth of its volume
A mesh of proteins called the lamina lines its inner membrane and gives it shape
Tightly packed, dark-staining DNA called heterochromatin tends to cluster along the inside of its envelope
Each pore in its envelope is actually a large structure built from dozens of proteins, called a pore complex

trap.title: The organelle, or its contents?
trap.body: The nucleolus is a real structure living inside this organelle, not just another name for the same thing — real answer lines specifically warn against accepting “nucleolus” as a substitute. Likewise, the DNA and chromosomes stored inside this organelle, and the ribosomes assembled inside its nucleolus, are each the wrong, more specific answer when the question is really asking for the organelle that contains and makes all of them.
trap.fix: If the clues describe a structure made of DNA bundled with protein, give “chromosomes” instead. If they describe the genetic molecule itself, give “DNA.” If they describe tiny protein-building machines, give “ribosomes.” Only answer with the organelle itself when the clues describe the whole envelope, its pores, or its “control center” role.
trap.line: Real answer line: Nucleus (accept cell nucleus or nuclei; do not accept nucleolus, DNA, or chromosomes)
